explain.say: A mushroom is only a small part of a fungus, like an apple on a tree. Most of the fungus is hidden underground or inside wood, and the mushroom pops up just to spread spores.

explain.say: It starts with a spore, a speck far smaller than a seed, landing somewhere damp with food, like soil, dead leaves or a log. The spore sprouts a thin thread called a hypha.

explain.say: The threads branch and spread into a huge web called a mycelium. It feeds by releasing enzymes that dissolve dead plant material around it, then soaking up the food.

explain.say: When conditions are right, often after rain, the mycelium pushes up a mushroom. Under its cap, thin gills release billions of spores that drift away to start new fungi.

faq.a: Mycelium is the main body of a fungus: a web of thin threads called hyphae spreading through soil, wood or leaves. It can be huge and live for many years, while mushrooms come and go.

faq.q: Is a mushroom the whole fungus?
faq.a: No. A mushroom is the fruiting body, the part that makes spores, a bit like a fruit on a tree. The rest of the fungus is a hidden web of threads.
asks: What part of the fungus is the mushroom?

faq.q: How do mushrooms spread their spores?
faq.a: Spores form on the gills or in tiny tubes under the cap and fall into the air. They are so light that breezes carry them far, and one mushroom can release billions.
No. Fungi have no chlorophyll and cannot make their own food, so they feed on other things. They are a kingdom of their own and are actually more closely related to animals than to plants.
Some are delicious but others are deadly, and poisonous ones can look almost exactly like safe ones. Never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has checked it.

facts: A honey fungus (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon spreads through about 9 square kilometres of forest and is among the largest organisms known.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
Fungal cell walls contain chitin, the same tough material found in insect shells.
